title: Size the result buffer from what the SQL returned last time
impact: `decodeQuery` starts every result at 256 rows' worth of `List<Object?>` slots and doubles when it overflows. Growing that list copies every live element with a store barrier into a freshly faulted array, so a 200k-slot result copies ~322k slots through ~5 MB of immediate garbage on its way up. A standalone AOT reproduction of the decode loop puts the doubling at 2318 us against 865 us pre-sized, with the loads, switch and stores together under 500 us — so buffer growth, not cell decoding, is most of what exp 251 measured as `Dart result construction` (2524 us of 5124 us worker wall on the same shape). `ReaderPool` now remembers each SQL's result size on the main isolate and stamps it onto the request; the worker consults it only when the buffer overflows, so a result that fits inside the initial allocation runs byte-identical code. Two design points carry it: the memory cannot live in the worker, because a result over `sacrificeSlotThreshold` ends the isolate that produced it and a worker-local hint dies exactly when it was worth having (that first version won 30-35% on mid-sized reads and ~1% on the largest); and the hint sizes growth rather than the initial allocation, because an early version that sized the allocation made a `LIMIT ?` statement alternating 8000/50 rows 2.8x slower on its small leg. Focused AOT A/B, two order-flipped passes, `ab_drift_check` REPRODUCED on every primary: 10k x 20 INTEGER -25.1% / -24.8%, 5k x 4 INTEGER -32.2% / -33.7%, and the repo's canonical 6-column product row x 10k -33.6% / -32.3% (3.5 ms -> 2.3 ms). Both controls return fewer rows than the initial buffer holds, so the changed path is unreachable and they move opposite signs inside the 3% floor; both mispredict guards are neutral by construction. Memory was not measured; arithmetic on the allocation path says total bytes allocated fall 14-61% everywhere (the intermediate arrays stop existing) but peak capacity is not a guaranteed improvement — 23.7% smaller on all three primary lanes, yet 22-25% larger for a result that lands just under a doubling boundary, as `mixed6-1k` does. This closes exp 059 as wrongly rejected rather than re-tested: its rejection reason was the April release suite's noise floor, its mechanism claim that `list growth is already cheap` is false, and it sized the initial allocation — carrying exp 067's small-query regression inside the same change.
